slides.visual_description: The Economic & Structural Reality — Understand the major economic and structural shifts shaping the current U.S. healthcare environment, including rising expenditures and the movement from independent practice to large-system employment.
slides.narration_text: To make sense of our daily reality, anchor first in the scale and structure of the system you work inside. Healthcare now consumes over 18% of the U.S. economy—up from about 5% in 1960—so every clinical choice is made under macroeconomic pressure. At the same time, the professional landscape has flipped: independent practice that once sat around 76% has shrunk to under 35%, while employment within large hospital or corporate systems has climbed above 50%. That shift changes autonomy, decision rights, and how influence actually travels. In this world, improvement isn’t about perfecting a single clinic—it’s about learning to navigate and shape a large enterprise.
slides.narrative_arc: From local practice assumptions to enterprise-level awareness through a combined view of spending growth and employment consolidation.
slides.script_notes: The Economic & Structural Reality — Understand the major economic and structural shifts shaping the current U.S. healthcare environment, including rising expenditures and the movement from independent practice to large-system employment.

slides.display_title: The Human Cost: System Waste & Burnout
slides.visual_description: The Human Cost: System Waste & Burnout — Understand how administrative waste and bureaucratic burden contribute to inefficiency and physician burnout.
slides.narration_text: Building on that structural reality, here’s the human cost. The inefficiency you feel is not a nuisance at the margins—it’s overtaking the work. For many of you, an hour with patients triggers nearly two more on approvals, documentation, billing, and compliance. That misalignment erodes purpose. Burnout isn’t rare; more than 50% of physicians report symptoms, with surveys placing prevalence near 54% in recent cycles. And the system pays twice—patients suffer when clinicians are depleted, and the tab to replace a single physician can exceed $500,000. Crucially, the top driver here isn’t seeing too many patients; it’s bureaucratic load. This isn’t a resilience problem—it’s a design problem, and that makes it solvable.
slides.narrative_arc: From recognizing inefficiency as a cost issue to seeing it as a human-centered innovation problem through linking waste, burnout, and design friction.
slides.script_notes: The Human Cost: System Waste & Burnout — Understand how administrative waste and bureaucratic burden contribute to inefficiency and physician burnout.

slides.display_title: Waste Beyond Cost: Administrative Burden as System Failure
slides.visual_description: Waste Beyond Cost: Administrative Burden as System Failure — Understand how a large share of healthcare spending is diverted away from patient care through administrative costs and waste.
slides.narration_text: The dollar picture matches your lived experience. Out of $4.3 trillion in U.S. health spending, preventable waste reaches into the hundreds of billions—approaching 0.935 trillion dollars at the high end. Administrative complexity is the single largest slice at 30%, with pricing failures close behind at 25%, then failures of care delivery at 20%, overtreatment at 15%, fraud and abuse at 10%, and coordination failures at 5%. Every dollar diverted to administrative overhead is a dollar not spent on prevention, treatment, or access. That’s the tension we must design against.
slides.narrative_arc: From recognizing inefficiency as a cost issue to seeing it as a human-centered innovation problem through linking waste, burnout, and design friction.
slides.script_notes: Waste Beyond Cost: Administrative Burden as System Failure — Understand how a large share of healthcare spending is diverted away from patient care through administrative costs and waste.

slides.display_title: Burnout as a Design Signal for Innovation
slides.visual_description: Burnout as a Design Signal for Innovation — Understand that physician burnout is framed in the source as a system design problem rather than an individual resilience failure.
slides.narration_text: Treat burnout as feedback from the system, not a verdict on individual grit. When skilled clinicians are overwhelmed, the architecture is misaligned. Rates exceeding 50% tell us the dysfunction is systemic. The root causes are specific—administrative burden, fragmented workflows, EHR friction. Each friction point is an invitation to redesign a process, a role boundary, or a tool. And clinicians fluent in systems thinking are uniquely positioned to turn those signals into blueprints for change.
slides.narrative_arc: From recognizing inefficiency as a cost issue to seeing it as a human-centered innovation problem through linking waste, burnout, and design friction.
slides.script_notes: Burnout as a Design Signal for Innovation — Understand that physician burnout is framed in the source as a system design problem rather than an individual resilience failure.

slides.visual_description: The Knowledge Explosion & New Technologies — Understand the acceleration of medical knowledge and the growing role of AI and digital technologies in care and training.
slides.narration_text: If burnout is the signal, technology is part of the response—provided it’s guided by clinical judgment. Medical knowledge now doubles on the order of weeks, not years, so static training can’t keep up. The good news is we have tools that reduce cognitive load and extend capability: AI-augmented clinical decision support to surface evidence at the bedside, immersive simulation to accelerate skill acquisition without patient risk, and real-time data platforms that shift care from reactive to proactive at the population level.
slides.narrative_arc: From awareness of accelerating knowledge change to readiness for clinically guided technology adoption through evidence, examples, and oversight needs.
slides.script_notes: The Knowledge Explosion & New Technologies — Understand the acceleration of medical knowledge and the growing role of AI and digital technologies in care and training.

slides.display_title: Why Static Training No Longer Matches the Pace of Change
slides.visual_description: Why Static Training No Longer Matches the Pace of Change — Understand that the pace of medical knowledge growth makes static training insufficient.
slides.narration_text: Here’s the core mismatch: the half‑life of what we know is collapsing to timelines measured in weeks, while our education architecture still refreshes on multi‑year cycles. What you mastered in residency can be partly superseded within a short span in practice. This is not a failure of individual physicians; it’s a structural gap. Closing it means building dynamic, adaptive learning systems—not one‑off courses.
slides.narrative_arc: From awareness of accelerating knowledge change to readiness for clinically guided technology adoption through evidence, examples, and oversight needs.
slides.script_notes: Why Static Training No Longer Matches the Pace of Change — Understand that the pace of medical knowledge growth makes static training insufficient.

slides.visual_description: AI Adoption Outpacing Oversight Preparation — Understand the mismatch between growing AI use in practice and limited formal training for safe oversight.
slides.narration_text: Deployment is outpacing preparation. AI is embedded in imaging, decision support, risk scores, and documentation across large systems, yet fewer than 10% of medical schools offer formal AI literacy. That asymmetry is risky. The concern isn’t that AI replaces judgment; it’s that uncritical reliance can erode it. Physicians need shared frameworks to oversee these tools, spot failure modes, and recognize bias.
slides.narrative_arc: From awareness of accelerating knowledge change to readiness for clinically guided technology adoption through evidence, examples, and oversight needs.
slides.script_notes: AI Adoption Outpacing Oversight Preparation — Understand the mismatch between growing AI use in practice and limited formal training for safe oversight.

slides.display_title: What the Upside Looks Like in Practice
slides.visual_description: What the Upside Looks Like in Practice — Understand concrete examples of digital innovation improving care delivery and clinical training.
slides.narration_text: The upside is not theoretical. Telehealth at scale expands access, reduces no‑shows, and frees in‑person capacity for complexity. AI‑assisted diagnostics in radiology and pathology now match or exceed specialist accuracy, accelerating time to diagnosis. Simulation‑based credentialing moves from time‑in‑seat to demonstrated competency, sending residents to the bedside better prepared. These are present‑day wins when the work is designed well.
slides.narrative_arc: From awareness of accelerating knowledge change to readiness for clinically guided technology adoption through evidence, examples, and oversight needs.
slides.script_notes: What the Upside Looks Like in Practice — Understand concrete examples of digital innovation improving care delivery and clinical training.

slides.display_title: The Consumer Shift & The Digital Front Door
slides.visual_description: The Consumer Shift & The Digital Front Door — Understand how changing patient expectations are driving the need for a frictionless digital care journey.
slides.narration_text: Patients now expect the same seamless digital experience they get from retail and finance. Miss that mark and you lose trust—and market share. A true digital front door makes access intuitive: on‑demand scheduling and messaging as table stakes, price and quality transparency for comparison, and continuity beyond the visit through smart follow‑ups. Intentional service design is what separates frustration from delight.
slides.narrative_arc: From viewing patients as recipients to understanding them as consumers through the design logic of the digital front door.
slides.script_notes: The Consumer Shift & The Digital Front Door — Understand how changing patient expectations are driving the need for a frictionless digital care journey.

slides.visual_description: The Leadership Gap — Understand the gap between physician interest in leadership and the limited availability of formal executive or business training.
slides.narration_text: Many of you want a voice in how systems run—about 70% express interest in leadership roles—yet only 5% have completed formal business or executive education, and less than 3% of medical schools offer business curricula. The result is predictable: up to 90% of C‑suite decisions are made without physician input. When that happens, choices about care delivery, resources, and technology lose the clinical anchor they need. The gap isn’t just career development—it’s a patient‑care imperative.
slides.narrative_arc: From interest in having a voice to recognizing the need for formal leadership capability through evidence of the physician training gap.
slides.script_notes: The Leadership Gap — Understand the gap between physician interest in leadership and the limited availability of formal executive or business training.

slides.display_title: Why the Gap Matters for Academic Health Centers and System Change
slides.visual_description: Why the Gap Matters for Academic Health Centers and System Change — Understand why the leadership and systems-thinking gap limits the translation of clinical expertise into scalable improvement.
slides.narration_text: Academic health centers hold the expertise to lead transformation, but expertise alone doesn’t scale. Without physicians trained in systems thinking, breakthroughs stall at the unit level. Three failure modes repeat: the translation problem—evidence never becomes workflow or policy; the accountability vacuum—no clinical owner for outcomes across the continuum; and the scale barrier—pilots that never grow because governance, finance, and change management aren’t navigated. Leadership capability is the bridge from insight to impact.
slides.narrative_arc: From interest in having a voice to recognizing the need for formal leadership capability through evidence of the physician training gap.
slides.script_notes: Why the Gap Matters for Academic Health Centers and System Change — Understand why the leadership and systems-thinking gap limits the translation of clinical expertise into scalable improvement.

slides.visual_description: Part 2 Summary & Knowledge Check — Understand the synthesized case for change: healthcare is increasingly data-driven, consumer-responsive, operationally complex, and in need of deliberate physician leadership.
slides.narration_text: Pulling it together: care is becoming data‑driven, consumer‑responsive, and operationally complex—and progress depends on deliberate physician leadership. Incremental tweaks won’t keep pace. Your clinical mindset already thrives in uncertainty; now translate it into system‑level action. As you leave, pick one burnout signal from your own environment and reframe it as a design opportunity—then outline the first test you’ll run to reduce that friction.
slides.narrative_arc: From separate trend awareness to a unified mandate for physician leadership through concise synthesis of the case for change.
slides.script_notes: Part 2 Summary & Knowledge Check — Understand the synthesized case for change: healthcare is increasingly data-driven, consumer-responsive, operationally complex, and in need of deliberate physician leadership.

A.visual_description: The Leadership Gap — Understand the gap between physician interest in leadership and the limited availability of formal executive or business training.
A.narration_text: Many of you want a voice in how systems run—about 70% express interest in leadership roles—yet only 5% have completed formal business or executive education, and less than 3% of medical schools offer business curricula. The result is predictable: up to 90% of C‑suite decisions are made without physician input. When that happens, choices about care delivery, resources, and technology lose the clinical anchor they need. The gap isn’t just career development—it’s a patient‑care imperative.
A.narrative_arc: From interest in having a voice to recognizing the need for formal leadership capability through evidence of the physician training gap.
A.script_notes: The Leadership Gap — Understand the gap between physician interest in leadership and the limited availability of formal executive or business training.

A.display_title: Why the Gap Matters for Academic Health Centers and System Change
A.visual_description: Why the Gap Matters for Academic Health Centers and System Change — Understand why the leadership and systems-thinking gap limits the translation of clinical expertise into scalable improvement.
A.narration_text: Academic health centers hold the expertise to lead transformation, but expertise alone doesn’t scale. Without physicians trained in systems thinking, breakthroughs stall at the unit level. Three failure modes repeat: the translation problem—evidence never becomes workflow or policy; the accountability vacuum—no clinical owner for outcomes across the continuum; and the scale barrier—pilots that never grow because governance, finance, and change management aren’t navigated. Leadership capability is the bridge from insight to impact.
A.narrative_arc: From interest in having a voice to recognizing the need for formal leadership capability through evidence of the physician training gap.
A.script_notes: Why the Gap Matters for Academic Health Centers and System Change — Understand why the leadership and systems-thinking gap limits the translation of clinical expertise into scalable improvement.

A.visual_description: Part 2 Summary & Knowledge Check — Understand the synthesized case for change: healthcare is increasingly data-driven, consumer-responsive, operationally complex, and in need of deliberate physician leadership.
A.narration_text: Pulling it together: care is becoming data‑driven, consumer‑responsive, and operationally complex—and progress depends on deliberate physician leadership. Incremental tweaks won’t keep pace. Your clinical mindset already thrives in uncertainty; now translate it into system‑level action. As you leave, pick one burnout signal from your own environment and reframe it as a design opportunity—then outline the first test you’ll run to reduce that friction.
A.narrative_arc: From separate trend awareness to a unified mandate for physician leadership through concise synthesis of the case for change.
